archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-first, run-stopping)
archetype.definition: A roughly league-average team by efficiency, built on a functional Geno Smith passing game and a stout run defense, whose 2-5 record comes mostly from losing close games rather than from being outplayed.

report.headline: A middling team with a bad record: close losses, not bad football, explain 2-5.
report.take:
The Jets are not the team that bottomed out last year. In 2025 they ranked 32nd in net EPA at -0.271 and were outscored by nearly twelve points a game. This year net EPA sits at -0.002, 19th, with the offense 15th and the defense 17th. That is the profile of a team hovering around .500, not a 2-5 team, and the Book has noticed: they have covered 66.7% of the time, seventh in the league. Every loss has been competitive. The point differential implies three wins, not two, and they are 0.2 in one-score games, 27th.

The offense runs through Geno Smith, who has started every game, and Garrett Wilson, who has drawn by far the most targets. The passing game is solidly above average at 0.121 EPA per dropback (13th) despite a line that gives up a sack on 8.7% of dropbacks (28th). The run game is the drag. Yards before contact of 1.99 (28th) and a 25% stuff rate (27th) say the problem is up front, not just the backs, and Breece Hall has been in and out behind Braelon Allen. The defense is split the same way. Its run defense ranks seventh in EPA allowed, it tackles well (6% missed, third), and it gets home, with a sack rate of 0.076 that ranks fifth. The pass defense still bleeds efficiency at 0.141 EPA per dropback (26th), mostly underneath, where short passes have gone for 0.184 EPA (27th).

The noise runs both ways. Close-game luck has gone against them. The +3 turnover differential on only five giveaways is unusually clean and probably won't hold at that rate. Penalties, at 8.3 a game (25th), have been a self-inflicted tax, with 156 penalty yards against Green Bay alone. The ugly game logs, a 12-point output in Chicago and a -11.3 passing EPA against Cleveland, came in the middle of the season, and the last two weeks have been the passing game's best stretch.

Where it heads depends on the schedule, and the schedule is brutal. After Las Vegas come Kansas City and Buffalo, plus Denver, Minnesota and a second Buffalo trip later. The underlying play deserves a better record than 2-5, but with this slate, better than the record still likely means finishing under .500 rather than climbing back into the race.

strengths.title: Passing game carrying a weak line
strengths.body: Smith has kept the dropback game efficient even while sacked at one of the league's highest rates, and a 2.92-second time to throw suggests he is extending plays rather than getting rid of the ball. The Miami loss was his best passing-EPA game of the year. This looks real, but it is fragile behind a line that just lost guard Dylan Parham.

strengths.title: Run defense that tackles
strengths.body: Opponents have gained little on the ground by EPA, and the defense finishes plays, with one of the lowest missed-tackle rates in football. That is a sustainable skill rather than a schedule artifact. The caveat is volume: Chicago, New England and Miami all piled up rushing yards in recent weeks.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Pressure alone is only middling at 22% (16th), but the sack rate ranks fifth, and the eight-sack game against Cleveland shows the ceiling. Losing Joseph Ossai and possibly T'Vondre Sweat thins the front, so expect some drop-off in the short term.

concerns.title: Line can't block the run or protect
concerns.body: Twenty-one sacks allowed, a stuff rate in the bottom six and backs hit almost immediately: this is a structural line problem, not bad luck. Parham, an 86%-snap starter, is out. The run game will stay inefficient, and drives will keep stalling on negative plays.

concerns.title: Soft underneath pass defense
concerns.body: The run defense is strong, but the pass defense ranks 26th in EPA allowed and gives up efficient short completions. Offenses do not need to throw deep to move the ball on New York. Against efficient quarterbacks, this is the most likely way for the defense to lose games.

concerns.title: Penalties and close-game failures
concerns.body: At 8.3 flags a game, the Jets give away the yards that decide one-score games, and they have won only 20% of those. Some of the close-game record is variance that should even out. The penalties are a discipline issue that has followed them all year.

trend.note: The passing game swung from strong in Weeks 1-3 to negative against Chicago and Cleveland, then rebounded to its best output against Miami. Meanwhile the run defense has started leaking yardage in three of the last four games.

nextGame.headline: Coin-flip at home: Jets' protection versus a ferocious Raiders rush
nextGame.body:
This is close to an even matchup. The Book has the Jets -1.5 with a 45.5 total, and both teams grade near the middle by net EPA. Las Vegas scores (26.1 a game, sixth) but can't stop anyone (28.1 allowed, 29th), and its offense is all Kirk Cousins. Its run game is among the league's worst by EPA and success rate, which plays straight into New York's best unit. The real fight is on the other side of the ball. The Raiders' 29.1% pressure rate ranks second and their 12 takeaways rank second, against a Jets line that already sits in the bottom five in sack rate.

Availability tilts against the Jets up front on both sides. Guard Dylan Parham (knee) and edge Joseph Ossai (ankle) are out, and DT T'Vondre Sweat (knee) is questionable after leaving the Miami game. Breece Hall (quad) is out again, so Braelon Allen carries the backfield. Linebacker Kiko Mauigoa is on IR. For Las Vegas, receiver Jack Bech has been designated to return from IR, while receiver Dont'e Thornton Jr. and tight end Carter Runyon remain on IR.

waysToWin.title: Make the Raiders one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas cannot run, and the Jets stop the run as well as almost anyone. If early downs force Cousins into obvious passing situations, the Jets' sack-finishing rush gets its chances even against a line that rarely allows sacks.

waysToWin.title: Quick game against a leaky underneath defense
waysToWin.body: The Raiders are the worst team in the league against short passes. A rhythm, get-it-out game plan fits that weakness and also blunts their pass rush. Wilson and Kenyon Sadiq on short and intermediate routes should move the chains.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas allows touchdowns on 78.6% of red-zone trips, 30th in the league. In a game this tight, turning field goals into touchdowns is the margin. This also suits a Jets staff that goes for it on fourth down more than anyone.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush wrecks a depleted line
waysToLose.body: An elite pressure team meets a line that ranks 28th in sack rate and is now missing Parham. Sacks and drive-killing negative plays are the most likely way the Jets offense stalls. The run game offers no relief, since yards before contact are already among the league's worst.

waysToLose.title: Cousins picks apart the soft middle
waysToLose.body: The Raiders' passing game ranks ninth in EPA and protects well, so the Jets' sack strength may not show up. If New York keeps conceding efficient short completions, Las Vegas will score the way it has all season.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers flip a close game
waysToLose.body: The Jets have given the ball away only five times, but the Raiders have the second-most takeaways in football. Pressure tends to produce turnovers. One strip or tipped pick in a game priced like this, combined with New York's late-game track record, decides it.

nextGame.watch: How the Jets' interior line holds up without Parham against the Raiders' rush. If Smith has time on early downs, the Jets should win the underneath passing battle.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency profile of a middle-of-the-pack team should produce more close wins than it has. A 0.2 one-score win rate and a point differential worth three wins both point to positive regression. The clean turnover sheet points the other way and is more likely to get worse than better. The bigger obstacle is the schedule. Kansas City, Buffalo twice, Denver and unbeaten Minnesota are all ahead, leaving the Raiders, the Chargers, Miami and Arizona as the realistic wins.

The passing game looks sustainable as long as Smith stays upright. The run game and protection will stay below average unless the line gets healthy. On defense, expect the run stopping to hold. The pass defense is likely to remain a liability against the better quarterbacks on the slate.
swingFactors: Offensive line health, starting with Parham's return

confidence.note: Seven games, consistent efficiency profile, but key injuries and a hard schedule ahead.
